catalog_quote: We preface this discussion by observing that roots in ɬəw̓ál̓məš are typically of the form CV́C, CV́CC or alternating Cə́RC/CəRV́C. All things being equal, roots tend to remain stressed regardless of morphological operations on them. There are however exceptions, which we have not as yet systematically worked out. The reader is referred to Snow (1969) for the best extant summary. ... Many of these suffixes have several variant forms not necessarily predictable by phonological rules. The stress on these suffixes may be variable. These affixes need much more research. ... náw= 'big' (takes primary stress; the stem it modifies takes secondary stress) ... Our arbitrary working assumption is that, barring other evidence, it is the root that is stressed in the resulting form, with the copied material unstressed. (Vowels in unstressed syllables may reduce to schwa.) ... It is not yet known how…

new_statements.quote: In particular, the rules governing the placement of stress, on polysyllabic stems in isolation and on formatives in strings, are presently indeterminable. Throughout the report, forms given in systematic phonemic orthography are marked for primary stress, and phonetic data are marked for primary and, if occurrent, secondary stress. [p. 6] ... Rule (1) applies to bisyllabic verb stems in which primary stress falls on the vowel of the second syllable of the base form: [...] With the addition of the suffix -wən denoting continuative intransitive aspect [...] or in the context 'past', the stress falls on the vowel (V1) of the first syllable of the stem, and the vowel (V2) of the second syllable of the stem is elided. [pp. 25-26]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds ɬəw̓ál̓məš with an empty rule and no existing stress statements. Snow adds the explicit finding that no placement rule could be established (stress lexically marked per form) plus one morphologically conditioned stress shift; nothing in the catalog is contradicted because the catalog says nothing.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Snow states outright that the rules governing stress placement, both on polysyllabic stems in isolation and on morphemes in strings, could not be determined from the 1967-68 field data (semi-speakers, mostly lexical items); every cited form is therefore marked for primary stress individually. The only stress rule he gives is morphological: disyllabic verb stems with base stress on the second syllable shift stress to the first syllable (with elision of the second vowel) before the continuative-intransitive suffix -wən or in the 'past' context, e.g. qeléq 'run' -> ʔiqélqwən 'he is running'. Long vowels shorten when unstressed (Rule 2, p. 27). Examples show stress on roots or lexical suffixes in various positions (e.g. sá·cat 'belly', sa·culác 'intestines').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Phonetic transcriptions are marked for secondary stress 'if occurrent' (p. 6); no rule for it is given. Reduplicated copies follow the stem 'and it is unstressed' (p. 53).
new_statements.exceptions: Rule (1) stress shift in disyllabic verb stems under -wən/'past'; unstressed-vowel reduction and elision not yet characterizable (p. 52); unstressed long vowels shorten (p. 27); reduplicant unstressed (p. 53). scanned note: the quoted text has small scanned corrections ('consider~bly', 'andt' read as 'and,'); the suffix -wən is rendered as '-\!ren'/'-~T~n' in the scanned.
new_statements.identity_note: Snow 1969 describes Lower Chehalis from 1967-68 fieldwork (Kinkade and Snow) with four non-fluent speakers, Nina Bumgarner, Lewis Hawks, Edna Olsen and Claude Waine, southwestern Washington (Shoalwater Bay / Willapa region); no sub-dialect is named. Robertson 2024 works from Kinkade's Lower Chehalis files (the epigraph is from Nina Bumgarner, 1978) and compares Upper Chehalis, Cowlitz and Quinault; it is an etymology of the word 'Chinook', not a description of the language.

sources.quote: Of Lower Chehalis interrogative/deictic roots: 'While these are stressed, as we expect roots to be, the data from one Tsamosan language, Qn, additionally include certain words ... bearing an unstressed prefix kə-'; also p.~495 an 'unstressed Lo prefix' nəkʷ- 'together'. Consistent with root-anchored stress and unstressed grammatical prefixes.

sources.quote: Only stress content: one root type (C-a-Resonant-C) has aspectual variants — 'The continuative of such roots has the stressed vowel preceding the resonant (CaRá- [sic scanned]), the completive has it after (CaRáC-, with an epenthetic vowel before the resonant)', e.g. ʔi-láik-n 'he is falling' / ta laiák-w 'he fell'. No general stress rule stated.
